title: The Tuesday Jamie Oliver's Restaurants Closed Their Doors
dek: On 21 May 2019, after two years of rescue money and a failed search for a buyer, Jamie Oliver's UK restaurant group called in administrators and 22 of its 25 restaurants shut.

story.company: Jamie Oliver Restaurant Group (Jamie's Italian, Barbecoa, Fifteen)
story.event: The UK restaurant group's collapse into administration
story.summary: On 21 May 2019 the Jamie Oliver Restaurant Group appointed KPMG as administrators after a search for new investment failed; 22 of its 25 UK restaurants closed the same day and about 1,000 jobs were lost. Oliver had put millions of his own money into the business from 2017 and backed a 2018 creditors' deal that closed 12 Jamie's Italian sites. Creditors were owed about £80m, the Gatwick sites were sold to SSP, and a 2020 employment tribunal found staff had not been properly consulted.
paragraphs: On Tuesday 21 May 2019 the Jamie Oliver Restaurant Group called in administrators from KPMG. Within hours, closure notices were up in 22 of its 25 UK restaurants, among them Fifteen in London, which Oliver had opened in 2002 to train unemployed young people to cook. About 1,000 people lost their jobs. Only three outlets at Gatwick airport kept trading.

The trouble was not new. In September 2017, Oliver later told the Financial Times, a phone call during filming warned him that the business had run out of cash and that he had two hours to put money in. By his account he put in £7.5m, then £5.2m more. In 2018 Jamie's Italian reached a deal with its creditors that closed 12 restaurants, and about 600 people were made redundant.

In late 2018 the group hired advisers to look for a buyer, and from January 2019 Oliver made another £4m available to support the search, the administrators said. No suitable investment came, and the directors resolved to call in administrators. Oliver said he was devastated and thanked staff who had put "their hearts and souls into this business". "I appreciate how difficult this is for everyone affected," he said.

The Gatwick sites were sold to the caterer SSP, saving nearly 250 jobs. In January 2020 KPMG reported that most of the roughly £80m the chain owed would not be recovered; suppliers, some councils, the bank HSBC and Oliver's own holding company were among those owed. In 2020 an employment tribunal found that staff had not been properly consulted before the redundancies and awarded claimants eight weeks' pay.

The Times estimated Oliver's own losses at about £25m. "I have to take full responsibility," he told the paper, while naming rent, business rates and labour costs as the business's worst enemies; he said no one had asked him at the start whether he had a plan B. Months later he told the New York Times that closing Fifteen was "the hardest thing I've ever had to do."

quote.text: When the flower fades, the master tenderly consigns it to the river or carefully buries it in the ground.
quote.source_title: The Book of Tea, Project Gutenberg eBook #769
quote.connection: Okakura's tea-master tends a fading flower as carefully as a fresh one. Oliver spent two years and millions of his own money trying to save his restaurants, yet the end came in a single day, once the money ran out. The passage asks for care in endings; the story shows how hard that is when nothing is left.

reflection: Most of us spend our energy on beginnings and on rescues. Oliver did both: he put in money, closed sites and looked for a buyer. Afterwards he said that nobody had asked him, at the start, about a plan B.

You do not need to expect failure to think about an ending. Something you carry now, a project, a role, an arrangement with colleagues or family, will one day stop. Deciding on a calm day who would need to hear first, and what they would be owed, is not pessimism. It is a way of making sure that if an end comes quickly, the people inside it are not the last to know.
invitation: Choose one commitment you carry, at work or at home, and write two lines: who would need to hear first if it had to stop, and what they would need from you. Then put the note away.

cross_checks.claim: On 21 May 2019 the group appointed KPMG as administrators and 22 of its 25 UK restaurants closed, with about 1,000 jobs lost
The administration followed a failed search for a buyer or new investment, during which Oliver made a further £4m available
In 2018 Jamie's Italian closed 12 restaurants under a deal with creditors, with about 600 redundancies
Oliver's own losses were estimated at about £25m and he said he took full responsibility
An employment tribunal found staff had not been properly consulted and awarded eight weeks' (56 days') pay
The Gatwick sites were sold to SSP, and most of the roughly £80m owed was not expected to be recovered

research_notes: Oliver's own money is reported in several overlapping ways. BBC (2019) says he put £3m in during December 2017; Al Jazeera gives $3.8m for 2017; Oliver told the Financial Times (reported by SmartCompany, 2018) that he put in £7.5m and then £5.2m more, the source of the widely quoted £12.7m; the administrators said he made £4m available from January 2019; and he told The Times (July 2019) 'I put in £3 million, another £3 million, then another £3 million, however the numbers went'. The Times and Restaurant Online, working from KPMG's report (secured loans of £18.3m from Jamie Oliver Holdings, £4.7m paid to HSBC, £3.5m of inter-company loans), put his total loss at about £25m. The story gives his own FT figures, the administrators' £4m and The Times's £25m estimate, each attributed. Jobs: early reports said up to 1,300 at risk (Al Jazeera, Consultancy.uk); BBC and the Guardian reported about 1,000 lost on the day, with up to 300 more at risk at Gatwick until SSP bought those sites, saving nearly 250 jobs; the story uses about 1,000. Creditor losses: The Times (via Restaurant Online, July 2019) said £83m; the Guardian (January 2020, from KPMG's progress report) said £80m; the story says 'roughly £80m'. The New York Times interview, read in the Irish Times's republication, converts sums into euros, so no figures are taken from it. Blame: Oliver's own words are used ('I have to take full responsibility'; rent, business rates and labour costs as 'our worst enemies'); he also told The Times he had been badly advised, which the story leaves out because it is reported only as the paper's paraphrase. The Unite union's criticism of rapid expansion is not used; the tribunal's finding on consultation is reported as the tribunal put it. Funding is set to 'mixed' rather than the slate's 'bootstrapped': the group was financed by Oliver's own holding company and by secured lending from HSBC, and no outside equity is documented. The Okakura passage describes how a tea-master disposes of a flower from the tokonoma; it is applied by analogy.
